t: At seventeen minutes past eight, Wren was looking for her other boot.
She was ten. She lived in a perfectly ordinary house, on a perfectly ordinary street, and she was fairly sure she had owned two boots yesterday.
Her cat, Noodle, was sitting on one of them.
That explains the smugness.
Noodle began a long, complicated stretch.
Halfway through the stretch, the house went quiet.
Not early-morning quiet. Not someone-has-hidden-the-remote quiet.
The clock stopped ticking. A spoon stopped halfway to the floor.
Mum?
Her mum stood still beside the breakfast table, one hand reaching for the spoon. Her dad was frozen in the middle of spreading jam.
Wren touched her mum's sleeve. Warm. Quite normal. Except for the not-moving part.
This isn't funny.
Noodle rubbed against her ankle. Still moving. Still very much a cat.
Through the window, Wren could see her street and, at its far end, the school gates.
A cyclist balanced without wobbling. A pigeon hung above the pavement. Beyond the gates, the flag stood in a fold the wind had forgotten to finish.
It's everywhere.
Behind her came a small click.
There was a door under the stairs.
Yesterday, that had been a wall. Wren knew because she had bounced a ball off it and been told not to.
The door had a brass handle shaped like a curled leaf. Under it, a little wooden plaque hung at a slant.
You weren't here before.
Noodle sniffed beneath the door. On the other side, something rustled.
Wren opened the door a little.
No cupboard. No pipes. No stairs.
A wood. A real wood, with a narrow path and enormous roots, where the air smelled of wet leaves.
A moth landed on the handle. It folded its wings. It unfolded them.
You're moving.
Wren pulled on both boots and took her coat from its hook. Whatever was out there, it wasn't the kitchen.
She checked the little torch in her coat pocket. It worked.
Noodle slipped past her and sat on the first root, looking back.
We're staying together.
Wren stepped into the wood. The floorboards became moss beneath her feet.
She looked back. The open door still showed her hallway, the stopped clock, and the umbrella stand.
She wedged a smooth stone against the door. Noodle batted it once, to check.
Well. That's definitely not the cupboard.
Wren looked behind her. Then at the trees. Then down at the cat.
You can TALK?
Apparently.
Since when?
Since the cupboard became a forest. I'm having quite a morning too.
The cat tried a small meow, then looked surprised all over again.
Both still work. Convenient.

The cat's ears turned towards a rustling sheet nailed to a tree. Wren stepped closer to inspect the rather odd notice. A portrait of a crowned woman occupied most of it. The instructions had been squeezed in underneath.
She stopped time?
That's what she's taking credit for. Queen Malvina. Modest portrait.
And she's keeping the Minute Key. We need that to start the Great Clock again.
For applause?
I don't think she'd enjoy being ignored.
Are they all right? My family?
Wren found a smaller paragraph at the bottom of the notice and read it twice. The cat leaned against her boot.
It says paused people don't feel time passing. They aren't waiting or hurting.
Then they're still at breakfast. We need to get that clock going.
Why aren't we stopped? Why can you talk?
I don't know. Yesterday I thought the washing machine was the strangest thing in the house.
Wren glanced back at the small rectangle of hallway between the trees.
Then I'm finding her. I want everyone back.
A corner of the notice lifted in the breeze. There was a little palace map printed on the back.
Wren lifted the notice off its nail and spread it on a flat root.
Across the wood. Get the key. Turn it in the clock. That's where we start.
Together. I recommend the path over the brambles.
Wren marked their home door on the map and folded it into her pocket. She switched on her torch.
Wren and the cat followed the path. A few minutes later, they reached a fork. Wren stopped to read the signpost.
The cat sniffed a suspicious bush and began an indignant meow.
Halfway out, the sound turned into a tiny trumpet blast. Something bright zipped from the cat's mouth into the bush.
That is not your normal noise.
A small patchwork imp climbed out of the bush and onto a wooden crate. He had mismatched button eyes and a jar full of glowing sounds.
His badge supplied an introduction.
Inside Echo's jar, one furious meow bounced against the glass.
That's your meow in there.
I can explain my displeasure. I would also like to make the noise.
Give the meow back.
Win it back. I've always wanted a contest.
He unfolded a judge's stand. Three paper stars dangled from it.
I want the meow. He wants an audition. Rather different errands.
Go on, then. Impress me.
Echo frees his sleeve. He points at Wren with the authority of someone standing on borrowed furniture.
Well? What have you got to say for yourself?
I'd—
Nobody asked you.
Echo balances his last star on top of his head. This does not make the stand look more official.
You're not very good at this.
Noodle meowed. A perfectly ordinary meow.
I preferred the trumpet.
Noodle sat on the trumpet.
Wren checked the signpost again.
The directions had become even less certain.
Echo had stolen the directions too.
The directions. Those belong here.
I might remember them if someone gave me a proper argument.
He pulled a little wheeled stage from behind the bush.
One wheel squeaked. Another squeaked in reply.
Meow recovered. Now, where were we going before all that?
I liked you better when you weren't talking.
Wren spots an old bridge drawn on the map. Beyond it, a road curls towards the palace.
Oh, off to save tomorrow? You think you're some big hero?
The actual path is visible now. Small pale mushrooms mark the way to the bridge. Wren starts along it.
Walk away and I get the last word!
The directions. You asked for these.
He uncorked the jar.
Three glowing arrows flew out, zipped back to the signpost, and pointed firmly towards the bridge.
I stole them. That was rotten.
Yes.
I know the palace road. Could I come as far as the bridge?
No stealing voices. No contests unless we say yes.
Can I keep the suitcase?
Is it yours?
Echo checked underneath.
It is now an excellent time to return a suitcase.
Ahead, a bridge creaked. Beside it sat an enormous troll in a kettle helmet, peering through a little wooden inspection window.
He spotted Wren's feet.
Echo sighed.
He used to do hats.
His booth carried a sign.
Below it, in much smaller writing.
Wren looked at her boots.
They had mud on them, a loose lace, and no opinion about adventure.
He inspected a centipede last week. It's still waiting for the verdict.
We need to cross. The Queen's stopped time in my world.
He raised three HOLD UP signs. One was upside down.
His small sign says the inspection's optional. I recommend very little boot discussion.
Wren steps onto the bridge. Her left boot squeaks. Toastbrig brightens as if the boot has just agreed to an interview.
Wren reaches the middle of the bridge. Toastbrig wheels his desk alongside on tiny castors.
Wren stepped off the bridge.
Noodle followed. Echo came last, walking backwards to read the small sign.
Optional. That's a very important little word.
Toastbrig's desk bumped off the final plank and stopped in the grass.
He folded the inspection sign away.
For one peaceful second, Wren heard the stream.
Then he opened a second sign.
Wren's hands felt a little tight around the map. She loosened them.
You can be annoyed. You still get to choose the next words.
Three drawers popped open beneath the new sign.
Toastbrig pulls a pencil from behind the kettle. It is a fence post with a point.
Only one drawer remains open. The path winds towards a building full of painted windows and extremely fancy curtains. Toastbrig lifts a little stamp. Wren isn't running. She is quite ready to leave.
May I?
Wren considered this.
Once.
Echo gave one magnificent squeak.
Noodle jumped, offended by the quality.
From the bridge came a distant shout:
Wren kept walking.
The boots kept working.
The building ahead had an enormous velvet door and a rather odd sign.
Someone inside the gallery announced a performance. It was the Duchess who owned the place, speaking loudly enough for the road to hear.
A very long silence followed.
Echo leaned towards Wren.
We could try the side door.
The road ended at the gallery's front steps. A garden path began on the other side of the building, heading towards the palace.
Echo tried the side door. It opened onto a broom cupboard.
Excellent brooms. Poor shortcut.
The cat followed a small arrow beside the entrance, then looked back at Wren. A narrow passage ran beside the main stage.
Through here. The garden gate is at the back.
By the entrance stood a rather odd sign. Someone had added a much smaller plaque underneath it.
Can she actually make us watch?
No. It's a public passage. We don't have to join the show.
Inside stood rows of empty velvet chairs. Painted people grinned from the walls. Three pairs of wooden hands clapped by themselves beside the stage.
A tall woman in a porcelain dress stood under the lights. A brass winding key turned slowly between her shoulders.
She spotted Wren and swept towards the footlights.
We're just passing through.
She pointed to her own enormous portrait. Its painted hands were applauding too.
I used to do my own judging. Limited appeal.
Wren reached the first row. The Duchess raised a finger; the wooden hands applauded before she had said anything.
The Duchess winds the key in her back one extra turn. It makes the nearest painted eyebrow spin all the way round.
Wren is almost level with the stage steps. The Duchess points at the remaining pair of wooden hands.
The passage led behind the stage. Ahead, Wren could see the garden gate standing open.
Beside it hung a casting board with three little shutters. Every role was still empty.
We're not staying for a second one.
She lowered her voice, as though offering a secret.
Noodle stayed beside the garden passage. Wren could leave at any time.
The Duchess points towards Echo. He is trying to free one button eye from a curtain tassel.
The Duchess produces a bright sash. The cat sniffs the trailing ribbon, then steps over it.
Wren reaches the open garden gate. The Duchess checks her last empty casting panel.
Outside, Echo stopped beside a watering can. Its spout was tied in a knot.
Your Majesty, a royal trumpet.
He bowed to it. The cat put a paw on his lowered head.
Wren laughed before she could help it.
Sorry. That one got me.
No paperwork required.
Through the open gate, the Duchess watched them. She looked at the watering can, then at her joke cards.
Wren didn't wait to see whether she tried it.
At the garden's end stood a signpost and a small newspaper box.
Royal deliveries. Somebody here must know where the palace post goes.
Then let's ask the courier.
Good. I want to get Mum's spoon out of the air.
Air is a poor place to keep cutlery.
A folded newspaper shot out of the box, bounced off a root, and landed at Wren's feet.
There was a picture of her on the front.
I haven't even met this newspaper.
From further along the path came the rattle of bottles and a voice announcing an extra edition.
The path opened into a clearing full of paper. Newspapers hung from branches like damp washing.
A delivery cart stood in the middle. A little green creature in a waistcoat balanced on its step, trying to catch a bottle that rolled from one elbow to the other.
He had long ears, ink-stained fingers, and a courier's satchel nearly as large as he was.
Do not catch it! That's Tuesday's scandal. Very sticky.
The bottle landed safely in the satchel. A second bottle popped out and landed in a bird's nest.
Much better. Birds can't read.
The bird turned its newspaper over.
Are you the Gazette courier?
Wisp. Delivery, printing, occasional corrections. Usually in that order.
Wisp's cart carried a sign, a row of rubber stamps, and three brass speaking funnels. He recognised Wren and reached for a fresh sheet.
Oh! You're her. The girl in the headline.
I wanted directions.
I can do directions. How newsworthy are they?
We're trying to get to the palace clock. Directions would be useful. Opinions less so.
Wisp holds up the paper Wren found by the garden. It shows a girl with Wren's coat carrying an enormous clock under one arm.
It says you stole tomorrow. Terrible business. Did you carry it in a bag?
Wisp puts the paper down. One of the remaining funnels whispers in his ear. He repeats it before thinking.
Everyone says you can't do it. You're too little for a palace adventure.
The final funnel makes a royal little cough. Noodle sits on a loose page. It is an ordinary, excellent sit.
It also says you and your cat can't even do magic. Go on, prove that one wrong.
Wisp lifts the cart's lid. Beneath the newspapers sits a little printing machine. Three bottles with royal seals are wedged in its rollers.
A fourth, empty bottle rattles in a cup marked with Wren's picture.
That's where the headlines come from. Palace words in, papers out.
Then why say ‘everyone’?
It was on the label.
You still said it.
Yes. I did.
The cat crouches beneath the cart and sniffs at a small drawer. Wren tries its handle, but it won't turn.
Something useful in here, Wisp? Or more mushrooms with opinions?
The delivery map. Those bottles are jamming its catch.
We need to mark what goes back to the palace. Something that isn't another rumour.
Wisp takes a pair of padded bottle tongs. Wren doesn't have to touch the glass.
Wisp lifts the first bottle. Inside it, a small voice repeats the rumour about Wren stealing tomorrow.
I can tell you who has read it. Every tree, every stall, every—
Wisp lifts the second bottle. The voice inside sounds very grand and very bored.
Tell the girl the Queen has never heard of her. — Shall I send something cutting back? I could put it in large letters.

Wisp removes the last royal bottle. It has a little paper arrow pointing towards the empty bottle with Wren's picture. Wren thinks of her mum's hand reaching for the spoon. The cat presses against her leg.
It wants your reply. Something furious, preferably. They're saving space on the front page. What shall I put?
Wisp pulls a map from the drawer and spreads it across the cart. One route crosses the wood towards a narrow entrance beside a tall clock tower.
Mirror Lake, then the old orchard, then the clock entrance on the east side. That's where I collect the royal post.
And the key?
The Queen wears it on a chain. I've seen it when she signs the dispatches.
He takes a small delivery sketch from his satchel and places it beside the map.
There's the outside-world dial. It stopped at the same minute on every delivery.
Seventeen past eight.
For a moment, nobody makes a joke.
Now we know where to go.
Why did the door pick our house?
What door?
Very new door. Very old trees on the other side.
I don't deliver doors.
Wisp checks his satchel anyway. The cat checks it too.
Definitely not.
I printed something false about you. I'll collect the old copies and put the correction where they were.
Thank you. No new quotes.
No new quotes.
He hands Wren the map. He stays with his cart to do the correction work; he does not become another travelling companion.
Wren, Noodle, and Echo take the lake path. Behind them, Wisp's machine begins to print again, more slowly this time.
I could have been a newspaper.
You'd get bored of being folded.
Fair objection.
At the lake, the trees and Echo are reflected perfectly. So is Noodle, although the reflected cat looks mildly disappointed with the arrangement.
Wren's reflection is already standing up.
You're late. I could have got there by now.
I haven't even sat down.
Wren's reflection stood on the lake before Wren had reached the edge.
The reflection stepped onto a flat stone. It wore Wren's coat, except every button gleamed and neither boot had ever met mud.
Wren lifted a hand. The reflection didn't.
I'm the version that gets everything right.
You've borrowed the coat. The introduction needs work.
A rather fussy sign stood beside the lake. The reflection straightened it, then straightened it again.
Do we need its permission to cross?
No. I've crossed here. Those stones go to the orchard path.
He pointed to the broad stepping stones. The cat put one paw on the nearest one. It stayed exactly where a stone should.
Of course you can cross. I'm offering to improve the person doing it.
Three gilt frames rose above the water. In each stood a tiny, flawless imitation of Wren doing something impressive.
We need the other bank. Not a replacement Wren.
Wren unfolds Wisp's map. A muddy thumbprint covers one corner.
Look at you. Muddy boots, grubby map. Some grand adventurer.

The reflection's second frame shows a miniature Wren arriving alone under a shower of confetti. The actual Wren waits on a broad stone while Echo folds a corner of the map back for her. She grips the map a little tighter. The cat waits beside her.
You've had help at every turn. What can you actually do on your own?
Wren pauses to check which stone the route follows. The reflection's last frame shows a tiny compass pointing everywhere at once.
You don't even know what you're doing.
The stones widened into a little resting place near the far bank. Beyond it, a dry path climbed between apple trees.
Wren sat for a moment. The reflection sat too, but not on the same beat.
You're quite bad at being a reflection.
I'm an improvement. There's a difference.
Three small rehearsal slates stood by the landing. The reflection tapped one with a perfect finger.
We could start again. This time, properly.
Or we could finish our walk. A neglected possibility.
The reflection stands beside the next stone and looks Wren up and down.
Most of that was luck. Name one thing you've actually done right.
Wren stands. The reflection straightens its own spotless coat and smiles without warmth. For a moment, Wren forgets the line she meant to say. The cat brushes her boot and waits.
You call that brave? You don't look brave. You look like you wish the cat could do it for you.
The orchard path is one broad step away. The reflection reaches towards its last slate.
One mistake and we start this whole performance again. You wouldn't want to get it wrong.
Wren looked back at the lake. Her real reflection had muddy boots, a crooked coat, and a map corner sticking out of her pocket.
She waved. It waved back.
I'll keep that one.
The cat peered into the water. Its reflection began washing a paw at exactly the right moment.
Excellent. A qualified cat.
Mine's got my good eye.
You've both got the same eyes.
Generous of it.
Wren checked the route. The orchard began just ahead. Beyond its branches, the palace clock tower stood against the sky.
Closer.
She folded the map carefully. It still had the muddy thumbprint.
Useful map. Mud included.
Under the first apple tree stood a little stage. Two wooden figures popped up behind it, one tall, one round.
Oh, look. The hero.
We ordered a better one.
They bowed to each other. A pair of folding chairs clapped shut in the grass.
Ah. The orchard act.
The orchard trees had been trained into arches. Beneath them, apples rolled gently downhill into padded baskets.
Beside the road stood a small stage on wheels. Two wooden puppets leaned over its rail, checking whether Wren was looking.
The tall one had a square head and a green waistcoat. The round one wore purple and stood on a box to be the same height.
Pip. Royal usher. Lead performer.
Pop. Royal usher. Better performer.
That is under review.
By me. Approved.
They flourished their hands at a rather crowded sign beside the booth.
We're using the road to the clock entrance.
Then you've come through our audience.
Congratulations. Best seat in the orchard.
Three pairs of empty chairs unfolded in the grass. An apple rolled onto the nearest seat.
Somebody's already taken it.
Wren stopped beside the route marker to check Wisp's map. The puppets swung their stage a little towards her. The road stayed clear.
The delivery path goes through here. You don't need a ticket.
Another big hero who needs directions to a sign.
Perhaps the cat should be in charge.
Wren finds the orchard on the map. Pip leans towards his little speaking trumpet.
Let's hear your great plan.
No, let me guess. Follow the cat and hope?
Don't interrupt my insult.
Wren folds the map. The public road curves between the baskets; its turn is clear now.
All that checking. You're not much of an adventurer.
More of a lost parcel.
At the far end of the orchard, Echo stopped by a service marker. Beyond it, a short path led to the palace's east entrance.
Wisp's mark is on the back. Let me check.
While he turned the marker's little panel, wheels rattled along a parallel track beside the road.
Please don't be another stage.
It was the same stage. Pip and Pop had rolled it to their official usher station. This side had three tickets clipped to a rail and a very small complaints box.
Second position. Royal duty.
Different backdrop. Fresh material.
Same wheels.
Pip and Pop wheel a small tarnished trophy between them, and Pop hands out voting tickets for the Which-Usher-Is-Better contest.
Between us, I'm the clever one.
She can tell. Go on. Which of us is better?
There's a correct answer.

Echo finds the delivery seal on the marker and compares it to the map. Pip leans towards Wren while Pop pretends to study the apples. Wren feels her face grow warm. The cat doesn't fill the silence for her.
You're all right when you stop letting that cat feed you lines.
Yes. Try having a thought of your own.
The marker matches Wisp's map. Wren's route is ready.
Found it. East clock entrance. Delivery path, just there.
Off before we've finished?
Typical. Not one decent answer between the lot of you.
At the last bend, Wren glanced back. Pip was holding open a basket while Pop moved an apple off a chair.
Our audience has practical needs.
So does our employer. She pays us to keep this road clear.
We may have misunderstood our duties.
Wren didn't wait for them to agree about that either.
The palace wall rose beyond the trees. Beside its clock tower stood a narrow archway with the same delivery seal as Wisp's map.
That's it.
Actual destination. No scorecard.
My favourite kind.
Through the open archway, Wren could see a corridor full of tall mirrors. Each wore a little crown at the top.
One mirror tilted towards her and bowed so low its frame nearly touched the floor.
The cat's ears turned sideways.
We're here for the clock.
The first mirror bowed until its little crown nearly touched the floor.
The mirror straightened on its hinged stand. Its silver frame had two thin brass arms and a crown much too large for its top rail.
We have quite a collection.
Tall mirrors stood down both sides of the corridor. Every one reflected Wren normally, then leaned in a little to see whether she was impressed.
Gleam raised a cushion bearing a bright little medal. Three long ribbons ran from the cushion to a desk covered in forms.
What's attached to it?
Only tradition. And a short acceptance speech.
The ribbon seems to have paperwork.
Such a clever, brave girl. Surely you'll sign one little statement saying our Queen has treated you wonderfully.
Gleam tilts the cushion so the medal catches the light. A rather long tag unfolds beneath it.
It's a gift. Completely free. Just wear it during the Queen's three-hour appreciation ceremony.
Wren glances at the path beyond the desk. Echo has found the small clock symbol on its wall.
After all our lovely words, you could show a little gratitude. Don't be difficult.
Beyond the desk stood a low service table. On it lay a booklet with a clock and a little open door on its cover.
Clock instructions. Could be useful.
I wish we'd had those at breakfast.
Wren opened the booklet. Its first diagram showed a stopped clock, one loose shining second, and a small doorway.
It leaves someone moving. A safety catch. And it makes a door for them.
Sensible clock.
Anyone touching at that instant comes along. I was lifting you off my boot.
A highly important sit, in retrospect.
So it could have been anyone.
It happened to be us.
The next page showed the Minute Key turning in a keyhole. A small wheel folded behind a metal plate and stayed there.
Turn it to return. It takes the key inside and removes the stopping control.
So she can't do it again.
And the first outside tick waits until we're through our door.
Breakfast will keep.
Wren traced the drawing once with a finger, then turned the page.
Near the back was a picture of an animal speaking on one side of a doorway and leaving pawprints on the other.
Oh.
What?
The words stay here. When we go home, you might not be able to talk.
Noodle read the little paragraph. His tail grew still.
That would explain how I started.
I don't like the other part.
No. Me neither.
Wren sat on the edge of the bench. Noodle leaned against her knee.
You'll still be you?
The page says so. Same cat. Same memories. Same excellent opinions about your breakfast.
I want to hear the opinions.
I know.
They sat there for a little while. Echo quietly put the booklet's loose ribbon between the pages.
The way to the clock-room door is still there whenever she stands. It isn't going anywhere.
Gleam rolls up beside the service table. He has brought a lectern with three small brass counters. The open clock passage remains behind him.
The Queen gets so disappointed when people leave. Surely you can stay and keep her happy.

A small plain mirror leans from an open shelf beside the table. It has no crown or forms. Its little frame faces Wren rather than the lectern. Gleam looks irritated that it has failed to request anything.
The service passage led to the clock-room entrance. Gleam held out a printed card with both brass hands.
Learn this before you enter. You're to apologise for coming, praise the Queen, and let her decide what you deserve.
Through a narrow window, Wren saw the outside-world clock face, its hands held at seventeen minutes past eight.
Below the window stood the real keyhole from the booklet, with a small lever behind clear glass.
There it is. Same drawing. Same mechanism.
Now we need the key.
One job left.
A velvet curtain divided the clock platform from a much larger room. Behind it, someone adjusted a microphone that didn't need electricity.
Move the throne forward. A little more. No, I should be larger than the clock.
A wooden wheel squeaked. Something very grand bumped into something very practical.
Who put a clock in my clock room?
Wren drew the curtain aside.
The woman from the royal notice sat on a throne mounted on wheels. Her crown was real. So was the small key on the chain around her neck.
Behind her waited painted spectators, a rack of applause paddles, and three splendid reservation pennants. The seats in front were empty.
Queen Malvina the Magnificent. You may begin being impressed.
You stopped my world.
And at last, someone came to see me.
Wren looked at the key, then at the clock platform to her left.
I take the key. Echo, keep the booklet open. Noodle, stay beside me.
I can do a page.
I can do beside.
Wren folded her map into her pocket. She had come a long way to reach this room.
A few borrowed tricks and a talking pet. Is that meant to impress me?
Wren feels the old hot flicker in her cheeks. Noodle stays at her ankle.
Did your cat write that for you? How sweet. A little hero with someone else's words.
You got through a wood full of fools. Here, I decide what you're worth.
The Queen rose and wheeled a little display lectern to the edge of her stage. Three gold ceremonial seals dangled from it. Beside it, a clear walkway led to the clock.
You will kneel. I will display the Minute Key. Then you may thank me for considering your request.
She lifted the chain, letting the key swing before the audience that wasn't there.
Wren looked at the clock's keyhole. Echo held the booklet open to the return page.
Turn to return. The clock takes the key. First outside tick waits for you at home.
I remember.
I'll stay with you.
She's making a very big claim. Look for the bit that doesn't hold up.
You didn't win your way here. A cat fed you lines and a pack of fools let you pass. Take them away. What's left?
The Queen unclasped the chain and laid the key on the lectern's cushion. She spread both hands for the surrender speech she expected next.
Listen to you. Practising little answers while I hold your entire morning. One clever sentence doesn't make you powerful.
Wren is beside the lectern. The clock's keyhole is a few clear steps away. Noodle is at her ankle; Echo has the return page open.
Leave and all you've proved is that you couldn't beat me. Go on. Give me your last little line. Make it worth hearing.
The Minute Key fitted the clock exactly.
Return. One full turn.
Wren closed her hand around the key. Noodle leaned against her boot.
I haven't finished!
We have.
Wren turned it.
Inside the clock, something clicked into place with the solid, satisfying sound of a door being properly shut.
The key slid gently into the mechanism. Behind the glass, the outside-world stopping wheel folded away. A plain metal plate covered it.
Across the stopped dial, a line of light ran towards the tiny doorway symbol. The first tick was ready, waiting at Wren's home door.
Set. She can't stop the outside face again.
Good.
For the first time since the spoon stopped falling, Wren let out one long breath.
That's your morning.
The Queen reached for the applause handle beside her throne. One wooden hand unfolded, patted her crown once, and folded back.
That was not the response I requested.
Wren picked up her map. Echo closed the booklet.
You'll have to finish without us.
The three of them took the service passage out. Nobody waited for the Queen's answer.
At the palace arch, the home-door mark on Wren's map glowed. A ribbon of pale light followed the familiar road back through the orchard, the lake path, the Gazette clearing, and the gallery garden.
It's showing us the way home.
Return route. No inspections.
Pip and Pop lifted their stage clear of the road and tried bowing in opposite directions.
At the Gazette, Wisp pinned his correction above the old headline. He waved a clean sheet of paper as they passed.
No new quote. Just: safe journey.
Thank you.
Through the gallery gate, the Duchess was trying a joke about a watering can. Her portrait laughed a little too early. She tried again.
Toastbrig looked up as they crossed the bridge.
He checked his optional-inspection plaque and stopped himself.
They are.
Her left boot squeaked. The bird squeaked back.
At the first fork, the palace signpost's arrows all pointed where they should. Wren's home door stood beyond it, the hallway still lit on the other side.
I think I'll stay. This wood could use a directions department.
No stealing the directions.
Strong policy. I approve.
He unpinned one paper star from his old badge and gave it to Wren.
No contest attached.
I'll keep it.
Echo gave Noodle a small bow.
A pleasure borrowing none of your noises this afternoon.
Your restraint has been noted.
They touched a soft cloth hand to a small furry paw. Then Echo stepped back towards the signpost, giving them room at the door.
Through the doorway, Wren could see the umbrella stand, the clock, and the bit of her kitchen where the spoon still hung.
She sat on the moss instead of crossing straight away.
I know you're coming with me.
Of course.
I still feel like I'm saying goodbye.
Noodle climbed into her lap, exactly as he did at home.
To the talking bit. I'll miss it too.
What if I need you to say something?
You can ask. I might answer with a paw. Or sitting on the thing you need.
You did that already.
Years of practice.
Wren stroked the warm patch between his ears.
I liked knowing what you were thinking.
I was there before the words.
I know. I just liked hearing you.
I liked answering.
For a while, they only listened to the leaves. Wren had a small cry. Noodle stayed in her lap.
Will you remember?
The booklet said I would. I'm keeping the part where you took the key.
I was scared.
I was there. You took it anyway.
We did it together.
Yes.
Wren wiped her face with her sleeve. Noodle put one paw on her hand.
That can be our thing.
Paw on hand. Very manageable.
When I need to know you're here.
I'll do my best.
Wren stood with Noodle in her arms. On the other side of the door, home waited.
Ready?
Right here.
Wren stepped onto the hallway floor. Noodle's last paw crossed with her.
The clock ticked.
In the kitchen, the spoon fell with one small, ordinary clink.
Outside, a pigeon finished its wingbeat. A bicycle wheel turned. At the far end of the street, the school flag opened in the wind.
Morning, Wren. Found your other boot?
Wren looked down. Both boots were there, muddy right up to the laces.
She laughed. It came out with a little leftover crying in it.
Oh, love. Come here.
Her mum's arms closed around her. Her dad put the jam knife down and made room at the table.
Quite a morning?
A very long one.
Tell us.
You'll need to start with the door.
Wren opened her hand. Echo's paper star lay in her palm, with a tiny thread still tied to one corner.
Noodle jumped onto the chair beside Wren.
You can tell the bit about the trumpet.
He opened his mouth.
Wren's smile wobbled. She knew what the booklet had said. Hearing the little sound still hurt.
What is it?
I'm going to miss something.
You can tell me that bit too.
Wren rested her hand beside the breakfast plate.
Noodle set one paw on it.
His purr began, warm and familiar. Wren stayed there and listened.
She missed his sentences. She loved the weight of his paw.
Her dad put down a fresh piece of toast. Noodle looked at it with the concentrated hope of a cat who had never been fed in his life.
That one's mine.
Noodle looked at her. Then at the toast. Then very deliberately at his own bowl.
Yes. I still understand that opinion.
Wren laughed again. This time she kept laughing.
By the stairs, the new door had become an ordinary wall again.
Wren tucked the paper star beside her bed. Later, Noodle curled against her leg while she wrote down the adventure before she forgot any of the good bits.
When she reached the part about the key, she stopped and read it back.
I was scared. I took it anyway. Noodle came with me.
He rested a paw against her wrist.
Wren turned off the light when she was ready. Tomorrow was hers again.
